summary: Discusses differences between the IS-IS routing protocol as written in ISO 10589 and the way it is actually deployed. It is meant to help people who implement, test and deploy IS-IS. A companion document, RFC 3787, covers the IP-routing side described in RFC 1195.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS is a way for routers to share maps. The rulebook and real-world practice differ a bit, so this lists the gaps to help builders get equipment to work together.

questions: how does is-is differ from iso 10589
subtitle: Where deployed IS-IS routers behave differently from the ISO 10589 text, and what implementers should do about it.

tldr.problem: IS-IS as described in ISO 10589 has proved durable, but some of its original design choices have been modified in practice, so implementers, testers and deployers can be surprised by what appears on the wire.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through twelve topics, from constants that operators change to constants that never change, buffer sizes, padding, checksums, tie-breaking and the overload bit, and gives MUST and SHOULD guidance for each.
tldr.outcome: It changes no protocol. It records current practice so implementations interoperate, and a companion document covers the IP routing side.

today: RFC 3719 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records deployed behavior of IS-IS and adds no new protocol, and its security section says the clarifications raise no new security concerns.

sections.title: Theory Versus Practice
sections.content:
Interior Gateway Protocols such as IS-IS give timely information about the best routes in a routing domain. The original design in ISO 10589 has proved durable, but a number of design choices have been modified. This RFC describes the differences between ISO 10589 and the protocol that can be seen on the wire today, as a service to people implementing, testing and deploying it.

A companion document covers differences between the protocol in RFC 1195, which carries IP routing, and current practice. The RFC uses the RFC 2119 requirement words, and it does not change the underlying protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The book of rules is good, but people changed a few rules while building real routers. This document writes down what they actually do.

sections.title: Constants That Vary, Variables That Do Not
sections.content:
Some values that ISO 10589 calls constants are changed in practice. MaxAge, the lifetime of a Link State PDU (LSP), is defined as 20 minutes with a recommended regeneration interval of 15 minutes. That is too short for some networks because it causes a steady flow of updates even when nothing changes. An implementation MAY use more than 1200 seconds, and MaxAge SHOULD exceed maximumLSPGenerationInterval by at least 300 seconds. It SHOULD NOT use its own MaxAge to discard LSPs from peers.

ISISHoldingMultiplier is 10 in ISO 10589, which means a neighbor must lose 10 hellos before an adjacency times out. Most implementations now default to 3, and values lower than 3 are unstable and may make adjacencies flap.

Conversely, some variables never vary. An implementation MUST use an ID Length of 6, and discard PDUs with an ID Length other than 0 or 6. It SHOULD use maximumAreaAddresses of 3, discarding PDUs where it is not 0 or 3. It SHOULD set both version fields to 1 and drop PDUs with any other value.
sections.plainLanguage: Some numbers that were supposed to be fixed get changed by network operators, and some numbers that could be anything are always the same. The RFC says which is which.

sections.title: Metrics and LSP Buffer Sizes
sections.content:
ISO 10589 defines four metrics (Default, Delay, Expense and Error), but only the Default Metric is used in deployed networks. Implementations MUST generate the Default Metric when using narrow metrics and SHOULD ignore the other three. They MUST treat the Default Metric as supported even if its S bit is set, because RFC 2966 uses that bit to mark routes leaked from L1 to L2 and back into L1.

IS-IS cannot segment PDUs, so LSPs must pass unchanged over every link, which makes a common maximum size essential. ISO 10589 sets ReceiveLSPBufferSize at 1492 bytes. The originating buffer size at each level must not exceed it, nor the link MTU. Newer information such as Traffic Engineering TLVs has made the space (256 * 1492 bytes at each level) a constraint, so raising ReceiveLSPBufferSize is possible, but a mismatch can cause routing loops and black holes. The RFC recommends consistent values network-wide, not enabling IS-IS on circuits whose MTU is too small, and reporting oversized PDUs rather than discarding them by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers pass map pages along without cutting them up, so every router must agree on the biggest page size, or some pages get lost.

sections.title: Hello Padding and Neighbor Checks
sections.content:
To catch size mismatches before a neighbor relationship forms, ISO 10589 requires padding of the initial hello (IIH) on point-to-point links. That assumed the link layer would reset the link if the padded PDU could not be delivered, but many links today lack that service. So if padding is used, point-to-point IIHs SHOULD be padded until the sender declares the adjacency Up, and padding SHOULD resume whenever the adjacency is torn down. Padding is not transitive: A to B and B to C working does not prove A to C would. The presence or absence of padding MUST NOT be a test for accepting an IIH.

On a point-to-point circuit with an established adjacency, implementations SHOULD compare the Source ID of a received IIH with the neighbor's system ID and SHOULD delete the adjacency if they differ. Because IIHs have no checksum, some implementations instead discard the mismatched hello to avoid needless flapping, and an optional checksum TLV (RFC 3358) can detect corruption.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers say hello with a big padded envelope to prove that big envelopes fit. They also check that the name on each hello matches the neighbor they know.

sections.title: Checksums, Corrupted LSPs and Doppelgangers
sections.content:
ISO 10589 says an LSP with a zero checksum, or an invalid checksum, should be purged. That proved disruptive. Implementations SHOULD treat an LSP with a zero checksum and non-zero remaining lifetime as having a checksum error and discard it, and most implementations simply drop corrupted LSPs as ISO 10589:2002 now says.

A doppelganger LSP is one with the same LSP ID, same sequence number and non-zero lifetimes but different non-zero checksums, so the standard rules cannot tell which is newer. An implementation may break the tie by comparing the checksums as 16-bit unsigned integers, and if it does it MUST treat the higher checksum as newer. The choice of higher is arbitrary but matches existing implementations. A purged LSP is always newer than a non-purged copy.
sections.plainLanguage: If two copies of the same map page disagree and look equally new, routers pick the one with the bigger check number. Damaged pages are just thrown away instead of causing a fuss.

sections.title: Complete CSNP Sets and the Overload Bit
sections.content:
A complete set of Complete Sequence Number PDUs (CSNPs) must cover the entire possible range of LSP IDs, not only the range present in the local database. The RFC gives an example with two systems, 1111.1111.1111 and 2222.2222.2222, each with LSPs numbered 0-89. A correct set runs from 0000.0000.0000.00-00 to 1111.1111.1111.00-59, then from 1111.1111.1111.00-5A to FFFF.FFFF.FFFF.FF-FF. Sets with a gap are incomplete. Strict adherence is needed for reliable updates.

The Overload Bit is set in LSP number zero by a router that cannot store all LSPs, telling others not to use it for transit. Because an overloaded router might become the DIS, implementations SHOULD NOT set the bit in pseudonode LSPs, and SHOULD ignore it when seen there.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router lists the map pages it has, the list must cover every possible page number with no holes. A tired router can raise a flag saying do not route through me.
